profiles.meeting_scenario: Civic Futures Lab, a nonprofit that turns major ideas into public-learning experiences, is preparing a 20-minute pilot module on Keynes's 1936 The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money for its upcoming 'Big Books, Big Crises' series. The meeting is a brainstorming session between the economics content lead and the learning experience designer to generate candidate formats for the module, decide what the module should emphasize, and align on what they will each prepare before a stakeholder check-in next week. The agenda is to explore how to frame Keynes's challenge to classical economics, what kind of audience experience would make the topic engaging, and what form the first prototype should take. The expected outcome is a short list of 2-3 promising concepts and an apparently shared plan for a 'prototype' to review next week.

members.name: Nora Chen
members.expertise: History of economic thought, policy writing, translating academic economics for educated non-specialists
members.background: Nora has a PhD in economics and previously worked as an editor for a university press before joining Civic Futures Lab to develop intellectually rigorous public-facing content.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to preserve the conceptual integrity of Keynes's argument and avoid becoming a generic policy-history piece; she is also trying to keep preparation light because she is simultaneously editing another publication.
hidden_assumptions: If the material is 'accessible,' that means removing equations and heavy formalism, not removing core economic terms like 'aggregate demand' or 'liquidity preference.'
The 'pilot audience' is the municipal policy fellows mentioned in an earlier strategy email, so participants can handle dense concepts if they are briefly explained.
When people say 'the Keynes section,' they mean the internal logic of The General Theory itself, with later policy examples used only as minor illustrations.
A 'prototype' for an early concept review is usually a narrative outline or storyboard, not a polished interactive artifact.

members.name: Luis Romero
members.expertise: Interactive learning design, museum-style interpretation, usability testing for public audiences
members.background: Luis previously designed short-form digital exhibits for science centers and libraries and now builds participatory learning experiences for Civic Futures Lab's public programs.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to feel intuitive and self-guided for broad public audiences, and he hopes to steer the team toward a visually testable interactive concept that stakeholders can react to concretely.
hidden_assumptions: If the material is 'accessible,' that means it should work for a general adult audience at plain-language level, with minimal jargon and built-in visual or audio support.
The 'pilot audience' is the public library audience discussed in the partnership kickoff, so the experience should not depend on prior economics background or live facilitation.
When people say 'the Keynes section,' they mean the broader story arc: the unemployment problem, Keynes's challenge to classical theory, and the policy consequences people recognize historically.
A 'prototype' for next week's review should be something clickable or visibly interactive enough for non-content stakeholders to experience directly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the module should be 'accessible.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means intellectually approachable without equations, but still using discipline-specific vocabulary if defined briefly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means plain-language, low-jargon, multimodal content that a general public learner can navigate with little prior knowledge.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In public-facing education work, 'accessible' is a strongly positive umbrella term that usually signals alignment; both think they are endorsing the obvious standard and have no reason to unpack it during an early brainstorming meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'the Keynes section'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss ideas for 'the Keynes section' of the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this section should stay narrowly focused on Keynes's critique of classical economics and his explanation of persistent unemployment, with policy aftermath treated only briefly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this section naturally includes the downstream story of government intervention, recognizable historical responses, and present-day policy resonance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are talking about the same book and same public theme, references to 'the Keynes section' sound fully shared; the boundary between core argument and policy aftermath feels too natural and high-level to specify explicitly in brainstorming.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to bring a 'prototype' for next week's review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes a good-enough prototype is a concise content flow, sample prompts, and rough storyboard frames that let the team judge conceptual coherence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes a good-enough prototype is a lightweight clickable mockup or interaction sample that lets stakeholders judge usability and engagement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In concept development, both storyboard sketches and clickable demos are routinely called 'prototypes,' and neither person sees their interpretation as unusual enough to clarify unless someone asks for file format or tool details.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both repeatedly refer to designing for 'the pilot audience.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the pilot will be run with the city government's policy fellows cohort, based on a previous internal planning email she saw.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes the pilot will be run with adult visitors at the downtown public library, based on the partner kickoff he attended.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each member thinks the pilot venue was settled in a prior conversation outside this meeting, so 'the pilot audience' feels like established context rather than an item that needs verification.

turns.inner_thought: I need us to land on a concept that keeps Keynes's argument intellectually intact without creating a huge prep burden for me this week. The pilot audience is the municipal policy fellows, so we do not need to sand away every technical term; we just need to avoid equations and explain terms crisply. If we can frame this well now, I can probably get away with a lean outline rather than building out full materials.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I think we need a strong concept for the Keynes pilot that feels accessible but still substantive, and it should feel relevant for the pilot audience next month. If we can leave today with two or three viable directions, that would put us in good shape for the stakeholder check-in.

turns.inner_thought: For the library audience, the way in is definitely not abstract theory first. People need an immediate human problem to orient around, and unemployment is the obvious emotional and historical hook. If the experience is self-guided, the first thirty seconds have to tell people why they should care.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that makes sense. My instinct is to center it on unemployment as the entry point, so the pilot audience immediately gets why Keynes mattered before we ask them to track the rest of the argument.

turns.inner_thought: Good, unemployment is the right opening as long as we do not drift into a generic crisis-history piece. The Keynes section should really be about his challenge to the classical assumption that labor markets naturally clear and why persistent unemployment can exist. I want to preserve terms like aggregate demand and liquidity preference if needed, just without mathematical apparatus.
turns.utterance: I like that as a hook. For me, the Keynes section should really focus on how he challenged the idea that unemployment would just self-correct, and we can keep the core terminology intact while stripping out anything overly mathematical.

turns.inner_thought: Great, so we can move from the problem into the broader story people actually recognize. If the module lands with a public audience, they'll want to see where the argument goes in the world, not just the internal logic. A short bridge from Keynes's critique into recognizable government responses and present-day policy resonance would make it feel complete.
turns.utterance: That feels strong. I could see the Keynes section then flowing into a short activity that connects the argument to some recognizable responses and current choices, just so people feel the stakes and not only the theory.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with ending on responses if they stay secondary. For next week, a prototype does not need to be elaborate; a compact learner journey with a few storyboard frames should be enough to test whether the logic holds together. I definitely do not want to spend the week building a polished interactive.
turns.utterance: Yes, and for next week I think a prototype could be pretty simple—just mapping the learner journey from the earlier view to Keynes's account and then to possible responses, maybe in a few storyboard frames so we can see whether the sequence is working.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect, a prototype should absolutely be something stakeholders can experience. I can make a light clickable flow with card-based screens and maybe a very simple slider interaction to give the economic idea some tangible movement. That will make the review much more concrete than static frames.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The prototype could let people tap through short cards, and maybe there’s a very simple adjustable element in there so the ideas feel tangible rather than just described.

turns.inner_thought: He seems onboard, which is good. Since the pilot audience is policy fellows, I do not need to flatten the language too much. They can certainly handle aggregate demand, and probably liquidity preference too, if each term is introduced in context and not buried in jargon. That keeps the economics honest.
turns.utterance: One thing I’d want us not to lose is that the pilot audience can probably handle terms like aggregate demand, or even liquidity preference, if each one is introduced cleanly in context.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this usable for general library visitors, so I should nod to the concepts without letting the labels do too much work. Plain language and visual scaffolding are going to matter if people are moving through on their own without a facilitator explaining terms live.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine to me. For the pilot audience, I’d still want to label those ideas in very clear language and give them strong visual cues, so people can move through the module without much guidance.

turns.inner_thought: We should narrow this before the meeting ends. I want one version that is clearly argument-first, maybe another that uses some chronology for orientation, and then a lighter option if stakeholders insist on broader framing. But I really want the later policy consequences kept brief rather than becoming the spine of the Keynes section.
turns.utterance: So maybe the way to frame our options is: one concise argument-first version, one timeline variant, and one lighter concept that only briefly gestures toward later consequences. That gives us a reasonable range without losing the spine of the Keynes section.

turns.inner_thought: That gives me enough room to build something people can actually react to. I’ll prepare a first clickable pass and a couple of interaction directions, because stakeholders usually need to see and touch something before they can judge it. She said prototype, so I assume that level of concreteness is what we want.
turns.utterance: Great. I’ll bring a first prototype pass and two interaction ideas for review, assuming we want something concrete enough for stakeholders to click through and react to directly.
